lines: A broker can lose contact with the one system that actually decides what's true about the cluster, while staying perfectly reachable to everyone else.
It keeps answering requests the whole time, confident in a view of the world that stopped updating the moment that contact broke.
Nothing about being reachable tells a broker whether its own picture of the cluster is still current.
Running a second system just to track who leads what meant operating two different replication stories at once.
Folding that tracking into the same shape already built for ordinary data collapses that down to one.
One replication story to reason about, one failure mode to understand, instead of two.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Two very different designs could keep every broker's view current, and only one of them is what actually ships.
Does the controller push each change out to every broker as it happens, or does each broker go fetch updates on its own?
answer: Each broker fetches on its own.
Nothing is pushed out proactively — a broker tracks its own position in the metadata log and pulls forward from there, the exact shape this chapter already used for fetching an ordinary partition.
That choice holds regardless of how large the cluster gets.

lines: Here's that same fetch, applied to the cluster's own metadata log instead of an ordinary partition.
A broker tracks exactly where it left off, and asks for everything past that point.
Nothing new had to be invented for this — it's the same pull this chapter already built.
That periodic fetch is doing double duty: it's also how a broker proves it's still alive.
One broker comfortably inside the allowed gap since its last fetch, left alone.
Another sitting well past that same gap, cut off from being trusted, even while technically still reachable.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal settles it.
A candidate that could never actually win an election keeps reconnecting and sending a vote request anyway.
Every single time, something about that request disrupts the current leader. What is it about sending a vote request that causes that?
answer: Sending the vote request itself bumps the cluster's epoch, before anyone has checked whether the candidate could actually win.
That epoch bump alone is what forces a disruption — nothing makes the leader step down automatically, and nothing about the candidate's actual chances gets checked first.
The problem isn't eligibility. It's that the damage happens before the outcome is even known.

lines: Here's that same flaky candidate reconnecting across a dozen rounds, run two different ways.
Sending a real vote request every time: the epoch bumps and the leader gets disrupted, every single round.
Checking first whether it would actually win before sending anything real: the epoch never moves, and the leader is never disrupted, not once.
A controller quorum can also grow or shrink without a full restart — an operator adds or removes a member on the fly.
But only one membership change is ever allowed to be in progress at a time.
A second request that arrives while the first one is still pending gets turned away outright.
Every number in this reel so far came from one real run of this topic's own toy controller-quorum model, happening just now.
The fencing gap, measured directly, under and then well past the allowed threshold.
The vote comparison across a dozen rounds, and the membership-change outcome when a second request arrives too early.
So: two separate systems collapsed into the one kind of log this chapter keeps reusing.
A fetch that pulls metadata forward and doubles as proof a broker is still alive.
A vote that checks first before it disrupts anyone, and a quorum that can change, one member at a time.
